openingProblem.problem:
In 1935 Italy was still aligned with Britain and France. By May 1939 Italy and Germany had signed a military alliance. In the same years Hitler told his commanders that Germany's future depended on winning “living space”, while Britain's Prime Minister described his policy as a long road to appeasement.

So what drove German and Italian expansion: the ideas of the dictators, economic pressure at home, or the choices of the other powers?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: which mattered most — ideology, economics or the reactions of other powers? Give one reason.
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Has your judgement changed? Which source or fact changed it, or confirmed it?

chunks.title: How far did fascist and Nazi ideology drive expansion?
chunks.body:
Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Within months, American diplomats in Berlin were warning Washington that Nazi ideology pointed towards war. In April 1934 Douglas Miller, a commercial attaché at the US Embassy, reported that the Nazis' fundamental purpose was the expansion of German territory and the growth of the German race until it became the most powerful nation in the world. He added that the Nazis wanted several years of peace only so that they could rearm. In February 1935 George Messersmith, now US Minister in Vienna, listed their targets: Memel, Alsace-Lorraine, the eastern frontier, Austria and the fertile lands of Ukraine.

The clearest statement of Hitler's own thinking comes from the minutes of a conference at the Reich Chancellery on 5 November 1937, recorded by Colonel Hossbach. Hitler told the war minister, the heads of the three armed services and the foreign minister that Germany's future depended on solving its need for “space”, and that history showed expansion could only come by breaking down resistance and taking risks. This matters because it links racial ideology directly to a plan for war, which meant expansion was a goal and not only a reaction to events.

Italian fascism also glorified expansion, but the sources show it differently. US reports from Rome in 1934–35 describe secret, large-scale preparations for a colonial war in Ethiopia, which Italy invaded on 3 October 1935. Interestingly, Hitler himself, in the Hossbach minutes, explained Italian expansion by economic motives rather than by ideology.

Ideology therefore explains the aims, especially in Germany. It explains less about timing: the decisions of 1935–39 also depended on rearmament, economic strain and the reactions of other states, which the next chunks examine.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Nazi ideology set the goal of expansion: living space for a racial community.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Hossbach minutes also stress economic need and opportunity, so ideology was combined with calculation rather than acting alone.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Observers saw the ideological drive to war as early as 1934–35.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were private reports by US diplomats who disliked the regime; they show what observers feared, not what Hitler had decided.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Fascist ideology mattered less than strategic and economic motives in Italy's case.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The secrecy and scale of the preparations, and the press campaign, show a regime that saw war as proof of national greatness.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the impact of Nazi ideology on German foreign policy, 1933–1939.
To what extent was Italian expansion in 1935–1936 driven by fascist ideology?
Compare and contrast what two sources reveal about the aims of Nazi Germany.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Nazi ideology set the goal of German expansion.
useItInAnEssay.prove: At the conference of 5 November 1937 recorded by Hossbach, Hitler said Germany's future depended on solving its need for space.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that expansion was planned as a solution to a racial and economic problem, so it was a goal rather than a reaction to events.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the same minutes also discuss opportunities and risks, which suggests that timing depended on circumstances abroad.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Ideology was therefore the main cause of the aim of expansion, but only a partial explanation of when it happened.

chunks.title: Did economic problems push the dictators to expand?
chunks.body:
Unemployment was the new regime's first economic problem, and it presented public works as action against it. On 23 September 1933 Hitler broke the first ground for the motorway from Frankfurt towards Darmstadt and Mannheim, a project the archive's caption describes as a means of ending unemployment. Public works helped, but the larger programme was rearmament: in March 1935 Germany announced an air force and reintroduced conscription, which the US State Department later described as sweeping away the disarmament clauses of the Versailles treaty.

Rearmament created its own economic logic. Douglas Miller reported in April 1934 that the Nazis aimed to make Germany the centre of a self-sufficient economic bloc in central and eastern Europe, large enough to defy a wartime blockade, with an agricultural self-sufficiency programme at home. This is the idea of autarky. In the Hossbach minutes of November 1937, Hitler argued that autarky could not be achieved within Germany's borders: food production could not rise much further, and imports used scarce foreign exchange. Because self-sufficiency was impossible at home, he concluded that the only remedy was greater living space in Europe. Economic weakness was thus turned into an argument for conquest.

Italy's preparations show a similar link between economic resources and war. In September 1934 the US Ambassador in Rome reported rumours that the government had set aside two billion lire for an East African campaign; in February 1935 he reported factories around Milan working day and night on trucks, tanks and artillery.

The economic argument is strong but has limits. It explains why expansion seemed attractive and why the pace of rearmament became hard to sustain, but the direction of expansion came from ideology, and the opportunity came from the weakness of others.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Autarky turned economic weakness into an argument for conquest.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The same documents show that the goal of living space existed before the economic argument, which suggests economics justified rather than caused the aim.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Rearmament was both a cure for unemployment and a preparation for war.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Public works and rearmament could have been domestic policies; they explain capacity for war, not the decision to use it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Italy's colonial war was prepared through a major mobilisation of economic resources.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The figures in the 1934 report were rumours, so they show the scale observers feared rather than verified spending.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the importance of economic factors in German expansion, 1933–1939.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Economic problems turned the Nazi goal of space into an urgent policy.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In November 1937 Hitler argued that autarky was untenable within Germany's borders because food production could not rise further.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that conquest was presented as the only remedy for an economic weakness that rearmament was making worse.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Miller's report of 1934 shows that the aim of a German-led bloc existed before these pressures became acute.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economics was therefore a significant accelerating cause, but not the origin of the aim.

chunks.title: Changing alignments: why did collective security collapse?
chunks.body:
Collective security depended on the League of Nations and on the great powers acting together. Germany broke away first: on 14 October 1933 it left the Disarmament Conference and gave notice of leaving the League. In March 1936 German troops marched unopposed into the demilitarised Rhineland, in breach of the Locarno treaty.

Italy's war in Ethiopia was the decisive test. After Italy invaded on 3 October 1935, the League decided that Italy had broken the Covenant and recommended commercial and financial sanctions. The sanctions did not stop the conquest: Addis Ababa fell on 5 May 1936. They did, however, change Italy's alignment. Italy and Germany drew closer in 1936, after the sanctions and after Italy's alliance with Britain and France had ended. On 25 October 1936 they signed a treaty of friendship, which Mussolini soon called the Rome–Berlin Axis. Germany and Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact on 25 November 1936, and Italy joined it on 6 November 1937. This is a causal chain: half-hearted sanctions angered Italy without stopping it, which pushed Mussolini towards Hitler and took Italy away from the side of Britain and France.

The new alignments mattered because they changed the balance of risk. A US diplomat reported in November 1935 that European states had no real fear of Italy but were “profoundly afraid of Germany”, and in January 1936 that German rearmament seemed designed only for aggression. Once Italy stood with Germany, Britain and France faced two revisionist powers instead of one.

The Pact of Steel of 22 May 1939 turned the political alignment into a military alliance. Then the Nazi–Soviet agreement of 23 August 1939, with its secret protocol, removed the danger of a war on two fronts. Each realignment made German expansion less risky, which is why the collapse of collective security is a cause as well as a consequence.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The failure of sanctions over Ethiopia pushed Italy towards Germany.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Italy's alignment also reflected Mussolini's own ambitions in the Mediterranean, so sanctions accelerated a choice rather than forcing it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Axis and the Anti-Comintern Pact reduced the risks of German expansion.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were political agreements; Italy did not join the war in September 1939, so their military value was limited.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Nazi–Soviet agreement removed the last obstacle to war over Poland.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Hitler's aims in the east existed long before 1939; the pact changed timing, not purpose.

howItGetsAsked: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the importance of changing diplomatic alignments in German and Italian expansion.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The failure of collective security over Ethiopia made German expansion less risky.
useItInAnEssay.prove: After League sanctions in 1935–36, Italy signed a treaty of friendship with Germany on 25 October 1936, the Rome–Berlin Axis.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Italy no longer stood with Britain and France as a barrier to German moves in central Europe.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Axis was political rather than military until the Pact of Steel of May 1939.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Changing alignments were therefore a major permissive cause: they did not create Hitler's aims, but they removed the obstacles to them.

chunks.title: Appeasement: a cause of expansion, or a response to it?
chunks.body:
Appeasement means satisfying a rival's grievances by negotiation in the hope of preventing war. On 3 October 1938, defending the Munich agreement in the House of Commons, Neville Chamberlain said his main purpose since taking office had been the pacification of Europe, and that “the path which leads to appeasement is long and bristles with obstacles”. He also stressed that Britain was engaged in a great programme of rearmament. At Munich on 29 September 1938, Germany, Britain, France and Italy agreed that Czechoslovakia would cede its Sudeten German territory, with German occupation beginning on 1 October.

Critics answered him in the same debate. Clement Attlee, who spoke after him, called the result one of the greatest diplomatic defeats Britain and France had ever suffered, a victory won by Hitler without firing a shot. On 5 October Winston Churchill said Britain had “sustained a total and unmitigated defeat”, and that Hitler, instead of snatching his food from the table, was content to have it served course by course. Their argument is that each concession taught Hitler that threats worked, which meant appeasement encouraged further expansion.

The evidence supports them in one sense: the Rhineland was reoccupied unopposed in March 1936, Austria was incorporated in March 1938, and in March 1939 Germany occupied the Czech lands in violation of the Munich agreement. Each success was followed by a larger demand.

Yet appeasement responded to German aims rather than creating them. Chamberlain's own speech shows that he linked negotiation with rearmament, buying time as well as hoping for peace. The strongest judgement is therefore that appeasement was a permissive cause: it lowered the cost of expansion, but the drive to expand came from Berlin and Rome.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Appeasement encouraged expansion by showing that threats succeeded.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Hitler's aims were set long before Munich (Hossbach, 1937), so appeasement did not create them.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Appeasement was linked to rearmament and was partly a policy of buying time.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Germany was rearming faster, so time bought did not necessarily favour Britain.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The unopposed reoccupation of the Rhineland was an early sign that the powers would not resist.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Rhineland was German territory, so many saw it as Germany entering its own back yard rather than as aggression.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of a parliamentary speech for a historian studying appeasement.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Appeasement was a permissive cause of German expansion.
useItInAnEssay.prove: At Munich on 29 September 1938 Britain and France agreed that Czechoslovakia would cede the Sudeten territory, and in March 1939 Germany occupied the rest of the Czech lands.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that concessions were followed by larger demands, which suggests that Hitler drew the lesson that threats worked.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Hitler had set out the aim of space in November 1937, before Munich, so appeasement did not create the aim.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Appeasement therefore lowered the cost of expansion but did not cause the drive to expand.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
sourceSets.focus: The impact of Nazi ideology on the aims of German foreign policy

provenance.creator: Douglas Miller, Acting Commercial Attaché at the US Embassy in Berlin
provenance.sourceType: memorandum to the Embassy, forwarded to the US State Department

sources.text:
The fundamental purpose is to secure a greater share of the world's future for the Germans, the expansion of German territory and growth of the German race until it constitutes the largest and most powerful nation in the world, and ultimately, according to some Nazi leaders, until it dominates the entire globe. The German people suffering from a traditional inferiority complex, smarting from their defeat in the war and the indignities of the post-war period … have to a large measure adopted the National Socialist point of view for the time being.
…
The Nazis are not satisfied with the existing map of Europe. They are at heart belligerent and aggressive. True, they desire nothing more than a period of peace for several years in which they can gradually re-arm and discipline their people.

provenance.creator: Scherl picture agency, Germany
provenance.contextNote: The parade of the armed forces (Wehrmacht) on the Zeppelin Field at the Nazi Party rally in Nuremberg.

provenance.creator: Colonel Hossbach
provenance.sourceType: minutes of a conference held by Hitler at the Reich Chancellery, Berlin, with the War Minister, the commanders-in-chief of the army, navy and air force, and the Foreign Minister

sources.text:
The German racial community comprised over 85 million people and, because of their number and the narrow limits of habitable space in Europe, constituted a tightly packed racial core such as was not to be met in any other country and such as implied the right to a greater living space than in the case of other peoples. … Germany's future was therefore wholly conditional upon the solving of the need for space …
…
The history of all ages—the Roman Empire and the British Empire—had proved that expansion could only be carried out by breaking down resistance and taking risks; setbacks were inevitable.

provenance.creator: George S. Messersmith, US Minister to Austria (formerly US Consul General in Berlin)
provenance.sourceType: private letter to the Under Secretary of State, Phillips

sources.text: There is no use in having any illusions as to what Hitler and the Party want. They have their eyes on Memel, Alsace-Lorraine and the Eastern frontier. They nourish just as strongly the hope to get the Ukraine for the surplus German population and to get the fertile lands which Germany "must have". Austria is a definite objective, with absorption or hegemony over the whole of Southeastern Europe definite policy. As long as Hitler and National Socialism remain in power in Germany, Europe will have to deal with these aspirations, pacts or no pacts.

questions.text: According to Source A, what were the aims of the Nazis?

points: To secure a greater share of the world's future for the Germans.
To expand German territory.
To make the German race the largest and most powerful nation in the world (and, for some leaders, to dominate the globe).
To use a period of peace to rearm and discipline the people (they were not satisfied with the map of Europe).

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about Germany in 1936?

points: The armed forces were large and well equipped, with ranks of soldiers and many military vehicles, suggesting rapid rearmament.
The army was displayed at a Nazi Party rally, before a saluting crowd under swastika flags, suggesting the regime linked military power with Nazi ideology and popular support.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying the aims of Hitler's foreign policy.

points: Value (origin): the minutes record a closed meeting of Hitler with his War Minister, service chiefs and Foreign Minister, so they show the aims he expressed in private rather than in public propaganda.
Value (purpose): the meeting was called to explain long-term foreign-policy requirements to the men who would carry them out, so the aims stated are meant to guide action.
Value (content): it links racial ideas (a “racial core”) directly to the demand for space and to the acceptance of risk, which is precise evidence of how ideology shaped aims.

Limitation (origin/purpose): these are minutes written by one officer, not a verbatim record, and Hitler may have overstated his aims to persuade or test his listeners, so they cannot establish a fixed plan or timetable.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and D reveal about the aims of Nazi Germany.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: clear, valid points of both comparison and contrast.

segments.text: Both Source A and Source D show that the Nazis aimed at territorial expansion: A refers to “the expansion of German territory”, while D names specific targets.
Both sources also suggest that agreements would not restrain these aims: A says the Nazis wanted peace only to rearm, and D says Europe would face these aspirations “pacts or no pacts”.
However, Source D is much more specific than Source A, naming Memel, Alsace-Lorraine, Austria and Ukraine, whereas A speaks of territory and the world in general terms.
Source A stresses racial and global ambitions and the German people's support, whereas Source D presents the aims as those of Hitler and the Party, which could change if the regime fell.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the view that Nazi ideology was the main cause of German expansion between 1933 and 1939.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands: focused, sources used as evidence, accurate own knowledge, synthesis.

segments.text: Nazi ideology was the main cause of the aim of expansion, because it defined Germany's needs in racial terms.

Source C shows Hitler arguing in November 1937 that a “racial core” of over 85 million people had the right to greater living space, and Source A shows that observers had seen the same racial ambitions as early as 1934.
This was soon turned into action: Germany reoccupied the Rhineland in March 1936 and incorporated Austria in March 1938, one of the objectives Source D had listed in 1935.

However, ideology needed military power and opportunity. Source B shows the rearmed Wehrmacht on display in 1936, after conscription was reintroduced in March 1935, and the Munich agreement of September 1938 showed that the other powers would make concessions.
Overall, ideology was the main cause of the aim of expansion, while rearmament and the weakness of the other powers largely explain its timing.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
sourceSets.focus: Mussolini and the causes of Italian expansion in Ethiopia

provenance.creator: Breckinridge Long, US Ambassador in Rome
provenance.sourceType: telegram to the US Secretary of State (State Department paraphrase)

sources.text: All information recently obtained points to a more general preparation for an extensive campaign in Abyssinia than has been indicated by the Italian Government in its various announcements. Supplies and military forces are moving clandestinely. Concerted effort is being made to prevent any information getting out as to the size or general nature of shipments. Movements are being made by night … I have been informed today from sources deemed to be reliable that 30,000 troops have left the port of Naples; that the movement now under way contemplates the use in Ethiopia of some 200,000 or 300,000 troops … Factories for the manufacture of trucks, tanks and artillery at and around Milan are working day and night shifts.

provenance.creator: al-Musawwar, an Egyptian weekly magazine
provenance.contextNote: The caption reads: “With his foot, Mussolini is crushing the dove of peace.”

provenance.creator: Breckinridge Long, US Ambassador in Rome
provenance.sourceType: despatch to the US Secretary of State

sources.text: There have been current in Italy—in all parts of Italy—for some time rumors to the effect that Italy contemplated warlike activity there. These rumors are generally to the following effect: that the Ministries of War, Air, Marine, Finance and Colonies were cooperating; that they had agreed upon an expenditure of two billion lire; that the Treasury had made provision for it in its budget; that military reinforcements specifically and variously stated to amount to 100,000 men, 200,000 men, and 250,000 men had been allocated for transfer there; that large and varying quantities of supplies, equipment, had been or were being or were about to be sent …

provenance.creator: Colonel Hossbach
provenance.sourceType: minutes of Hitler's conference with his military chiefs and Foreign Minister, Reich Chancellery, Berlin

sources.text: We were living in an age of economic empires in which the primitive urge to colonization was again manifesting itself; in the cases of Japan and Italy economic motives underlay the urge for expansion, and with Germany, too, economic need would supply the stimulus. For countries outside the great economic empires, opportunities for economic expansion were severely impeded.

questions.text: According to Source A, what evidence was there that Italy was preparing for war in Abyssinia?

points: Supplies and forces were being moved secretly, by night, and information about shipments was suppressed.
30,000 troops had left Naples, and the plan envisaged 200,000–300,000 troops in Ethiopia.
Factories around Milan were producing trucks, tanks and artillery day and night.
The preparations were larger than the Italian government's announcements admitted.

questions.text: What is the message of Source B?

points: Mussolini is an aggressive, violent figure: he is drawn huge and snarling, with clenched fists.
Italy's expansion is destroying peace: his leg, shaped like the Italian boot on a globe, crushes the dove of peace.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a historian studying Italian preparations for war in Ethiopia.

points: Value (origin): it was written by the US Ambassador in Rome in February 1935, about eight months before the invasion, so it shows what a well-placed foreign observer could detect at the time, without hindsight.
Value (purpose): it was a report to his own government, meant to inform the Secretary of State, so Long had little reason to exaggerate for public effect.
Value (content): it gives precise details (30,000 troops from Naples, factories in Milan working day and night) that show the scale and secrecy of the preparations.
Limitation: Long relied partly on informants “deemed to be reliable” and could not observe Italian decision-making, so the source cannot establish Mussolini's motives or confirm the figures.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and C reveal about Italian preparations for war.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands.

segments.text: Both Source A and Source C suggest that Italy was preparing a large campaign in East Africa: A reports 200,000–300,000 troops planned, and C reports rumours of 100,000 to 250,000 men.
Both sources also describe supplies and equipment being sent, which shows that preparations were material as well as military.
However, Source C presents these claims as rumours, whereas Source A reports information from sources “deemed to be reliable”, so A is more confident.

Source C focuses on the government's financial planning (two billion lire in the budget), whereas Source A stresses the secrecy of the movements and the gap between Italy's announcements and its actions.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent was Italian expansion in 1935–1936 caused by economic motives rather than fascist ideology?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands.

segments.text: Economic motives were part of the explanation, but they do not fully explain why Italy chose war in Ethiopia in 1935.
Source D shows that Hitler himself saw economic motives behind Italian expansion, and Source C shows a major commitment of state resources, with rumours of two billion lire in the budget.

However, the scale and secrecy of the preparations in Source A, and the decision to invade on 3 October 1935 despite the risk of League sanctions, suggest a regime that wanted a war of conquest for prestige as well as profit.
Source B, an Egyptian cartoon, shows how the war was seen abroad: as aggression that crushed peace rather than as economic necessity.

Italy continued the conquest after the League recommended sanctions, and Addis Ababa fell on 5 May 1936, which suggests that the goal of empire mattered more than economic cost. Overall, economic motives were a contributing cause, but fascist ambition was the stronger one.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
sourceSets.focus: Domestic economic issues, autarky and rearmament in Nazi Germany

provenance.creator: Douglas Miller, Acting Commercial Attaché at the US Embassy in Berlin
provenance.sourceType: memorandum to the Embassy, section headed “Economic aims”

sources.text: Germany is to be made the economic center of a self-sustaining territorial block whose dependent nations in Central and Eastern Europe will look to Berlin for leadership. This block is to be so constituted that it can defy wartime blockade and be large enough to give the peoples in it the benefits of free trade now enjoyed by the 48 American States. In accordance with this purpose, an agricultural self-sufficiency program has been adopted, foreign foodstuffs are being rigorously excluded or the imported supply secured in increasing quantities from Central and Southeastern Europe.

provenance.creator: German press photograph
provenance.contextNote: Hitler at the ground-breaking for the motorway from Frankfurt towards Darmstadt and Mannheim. The archive caption describes the project as a means of ending unemployment.

provenance.creator: Colonel Hossbach
provenance.sourceType: minutes of Hitler's conference with his military chiefs and Foreign Minister, Reich Chancellery, Berlin

sources.text:
Since, with the solving of the unemployment problem, the maximum consumption level had been reached, some minor modifications in our home agricultural production might still, no doubt, be possible, but no fundamental alteration was possible in our basic food position. Thus autarchy was untenable in regard both to food and to the economy as a whole.
…
The only remedy, and one which might appear to us as visionary, lay in the acquisition of greater living space.

provenance.creator: US Department of State
provenance.sourceType: Peace and War: United States Foreign Policy, 1931–1941, an official account summarising reports from the US Minister to Switzerland, Hugh Wilson
provenance.date: published 1943; the reports date from November 1935 and January 1936

sources.text: The United States Minister to Switzerland, Hugh Wilson, had reported to Secretary Hull in November 1935 that the states of Europe, while fully realizing and apprehensive of the dangers inherent in Italy's course in Ethiopia, had no real fear of Italy; that, however, they were "profoundly afraid of Germany". In a letter of January 1936 Mr. Wilson reported to the Secretary that … there was indisputable evidence of the magnitude and intensity of German military preparations … The idea was becoming prevalent, he said, "that German rearmament on this scale and in this tempo can be designed only for the purposes of aggression".

questions.text: According to Source A, what were the economic aims of the Nazi regime?

points: To make Germany the economic centre of a self-sustaining bloc, with central and eastern European states dependent on Berlin.
To build a bloc able to defy a wartime blockade.
To achieve agricultural self-sufficiency at home.
To exclude foreign foodstuffs or obtain them increasingly from central and south-eastern Europe.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the Nazi regime's economic policy in 1933?

points: Hitler personally took part in a public works project (digging the first ground for a motorway), suggesting the regime wanted to be seen acting against unemployment.
The event was staged with many uniformed officials around him and a photographer present, suggesting that economic policy was also used as propaganda for the regime.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source D for a historian studying European fears of German rearmament in 1935–1936.

points: Value (origin): it is an official State Department account based on reports by the US Minister to Switzerland, so it records what a US diplomat in Europe was hearing from European statesmen at the time.
Value (content): it contrasts European attitudes to Italy and Germany and quotes Wilson's own words, which shows how fear of German rearmament overtook concern about Ethiopia.
Limitation (origin/date): it was published in 1943, during the war, and summarises rather than reproduces the reports, so it is shaped by hindsight.
Limitation (purpose): as an official account of US foreign policy since 1931, published in wartime, it may select reports that show the US government had recognised the danger early.

questions.text: Compare and contrast what Sources A and C reveal about the Nazi aim of economic self-sufficiency.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands.

segments.text: Both Source A and Source C show that self-sufficiency, especially in food, was a central economic concern of the Nazi regime.
Both sources also look beyond Germany's borders for the solution: A describes a bloc of dependent states in central and eastern Europe, and C concludes that the remedy is greater living space.
However, Source A presents self-sufficiency as a policy already being pursued, whereas Source C argues that autarky is untenable within the existing borders.
Source A describes economic dominance over dependent nations, whereas Source C points to the acquisition of space, a more radical and territorial solution.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, examine the importance of domestic economic issues as a cause of German expansion between 1933 and 1939.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands.

segments.text: Domestic economic issues were an important cause of German expansion because they were used to argue that Germany could not survive within its borders.

Source C shows Hitler claiming in 1937 that autarky was untenable once unemployment had been solved, and that living space was the only remedy, while Source A shows the aim of a German-led economic bloc as early as 1934.
Rearmament linked economics and expansion: conscription was reintroduced in March 1935, and Source D shows that by January 1936 European observers saw German rearmament as designed for aggression.
However, Source B shows the regime presenting public works in 1933 as a cure for unemployment, which suggests the early economic policy was domestic recovery rather than conquest.
Overall, economic issues largely explain the urgency of expansion after 1936, but the aim itself, as the Hossbach minutes also show, came from Nazi ideas of space.

sourceSets.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
sourceSets.focus: Appeasement and the end of collective security: the Munich agreement, 1938

provenance.creator: Neville Chamberlain, British Prime Minister
provenance.sourceType: speech in the House of Commons defending the Munich agreement

sources.text:
Ever since I assumed my present office my main purpose has been to work for the pacification of Europe, for the removal of those suspicions and those animosities which have so long poisoned the air. The path which leads to appeasement is long and bristles with obstacles. The question of Czechoslovakia is the latest and perhaps the most dangerous. Now that we have got past it, I feel that it may be possible to make further progress along the road to sanity.
…
We have only laid the foundations of peace. The superstructure is not even begun. For a long period now we have been engaged in this country in a great programme of rearmament, which is daily increasing in pace and in volume.

provenance.creator: German picture agency (Scherl Bilderdienst)
provenance.contextNote: Munich. From left: Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler, Mussolini and the Italian Foreign Minister, Ciano.

provenance.creator: Winston Churchill, Member of Parliament for Epping and a former minister
provenance.sourceType: speech in the House of Commons debate on the Munich agreement

sources.text:
I will begin by saying what everybody would like to ignore or forget but which must nevertheless be stated, namely, that we have sustained a total and unmitigated defeat, and that France has suffered even more than we have.
…
They should know that there has been gross neglect and deficiency in our defences; they should know that we have sustained a defeat without a war, the consequences of which will travel far with us along our road … And do not suppose that this is the end. This is only the beginning of the reckoning.

provenance.creator: Clement Attlee, Member of Parliament for Limehouse (Stepney)
provenance.sourceType: speech in the House of Commons

sources.text:
We all feel relief that war has not come this time. Every one of us has been passing through days of anxiety; we cannot, however, feel that peace has been established, but that we have nothing but an armistice in a state of war.
…
The events of these last few days constitute one of the greatest diplomatic defeats that this country and France have ever sustained. There can be no doubt that it is a tremendous victory for Herr Hitler. Without firing a shot, by the mere display of military force, he has achieved a dominating position in Europe which Germany failed to win after four years of war.

questions.text: According to Source A, how did Chamberlain justify his policy?

points: His main purpose was the pacification of Europe and the removal of suspicion and hostility.
Appeasement was a long, difficult road, and Czechoslovakia had been its most dangerous obstacle.
Getting past the Czech question made further progress towards peace possible.
Britain was rearming at an increasing pace, so peace efforts were combined with preparation.

questions.text: What does Source B suggest about the Munich Conference?

points: The settlement was made by the leaders of four great powers, Britain, France, Germany and Italy, standing together for an official photograph.
Hitler and Mussolini, in uniform at the centre, appear as equals of the democratic leaders, suggesting the dictators' strengthened position.

questions.text: With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for a historian studying British reactions to the Munich agreement.

points: Value (origin): it is a speech by a former minister in the Commons debate days after Munich, so it shows that appeasement was attacked by experienced politicians, not only by the government's opponents.
Value (content): it links Munich to the state of British defences, showing that critics connected appeasement with military weakness.
Limitation (purpose): Churchill was trying to persuade MPs that the policy was wrong, so he had reason to stress the defeat and ignore the argument that time was being bought for rearmament.
Limitation (origin): it gives one politician's view, so it cannot show how far the public or most MPs shared it.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the views of the Munich agreement expressed in Sources A and C.

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 5–6 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands.

segments.text: Both Source A and Source C agree that the crisis is not over: Chamberlain says only the foundations of peace have been laid, and Churchill says this is only the beginning of the reckoning.
Both sources also connect the crisis with British armaments: A stresses a great programme of rearmament, and C attacks gross deficiency in defences.
However, Source A presents Munich as an obstacle overcome on the road to peace, whereas Source C calls it a total and unmitigated defeat.
Source A presents rearmament as progressing well, whereas Source C claims that defences have been neglected, so they disagree about whether Britain was ready.

questions.text: Using the sources and your own knowledge, to what extent was appeasement a cause of German expansion between 1936 and 1939?

model.bandNote: Illustrates the 7–9 band in the plain-language paraphrase of the IB markbands.

segments.text: Appeasement was a significant cause of German expansion because it reduced the cost of each step, but it did not create the aim.
Source D shows Attlee arguing that Hitler had won a dominating position without firing a shot, and Source C shows Churchill warning that further demands would follow.
Their warnings were borne out: the Rhineland had been reoccupied unopposed in March 1936, and in March 1939 Germany occupied the rest of the Czech lands in violation of the Munich agreement.
However, Source A shows that Chamberlain combined appeasement with rearmament, and Source B shows that Italy stood with Germany at Munich, so Britain and France faced two dictators rather than one.
Overall, appeasement was a permissive cause: Hitler's aims were set before Munich, but each concession made the next step less risky.
